text: {"overall_winner": "A", "qualities": [{"evidence": "Essay A acknowledges the opposing view ('Some people would have to agree upon the fact that these cars are a good and alternative investment...') and then rebuts it, while Essay B presents only one-sided support.", "quality": "Counterargument engagement", "description": "The essay anticipates and responds to opposing viewpoints rather than presenting a one-sided argument."}, {"evidence": "Essay A develops distinct reasons across paragraphs (loss of awareness, laziness, loss of control, blame for accidents) each tied to the position, while Essay B lists benefits without deep development.", "quality": "Reason development", "description": "Each supporting point is elaborated with explanation and consequences rather than merely asserted."}, {"evidence": "Essay A uses article details such as 'In certain states it is illegal to have driverless cars' and the question of 'who is to blame for accidents,' grounding claims in the source text.", "quality": "Source integration", "description": "The essay draws on specific details from the article to support its argument rather than making unsupported claims."}, {"evidence": "Essay A's conclusion returns to the core theme of driving as freedom and control ('Driving is a way to be your own person and control where you want to go'), creating a cohesive frame.", "quality": "Cohesive framing", "description": "The essay maintains a consistent central idea from introduction through conclusion that unifies the argument."}, {"evidence": "Essay A's body paragraphs each open with a clear topic sentence ('Next, driverless cars will make people become lazy') and stay on that point, while Essay B's paragraphs pile up loosely connected benefits.", "quality": "Paragraph organization", "description": "The essay structures each paragraph around a single, clearly introduced point that is then developed."}]}
